seo.title: Codex vs HagiCode: Features and Comparison
seo.description: Codex is OpenAI's terminal coding agent; HagiCode is a workbench that runs it. Compare install, ChatGPT plans, features and when each fits.

summary: Codex is OpenAI's open-source terminal coding agent, signed in with a ChatGPT account or an API key. HagiCode is a desktop workbench that runs Codex as its executor and adds parallel sessions, proposals and AI commits around it.

content: Codex is OpenAI's coding agent for the terminal: it inspects your repository, edits files and runs commands on your machine. HagiCode is a desktop and web workbench that runs Codex as one of its executors. It does not replace Codex, and it does not sell or host OpenAI models.

If you want a fast terminal agent on your ChatGPT plan, with scripts and CI handled by `codex exec`, stay with Codex alone. HagiCode is for when you want several Codex tasks side by side, a written proposal before each change, or one workspace across repositories.

sections.title: Codex vs HagiCode at a glance

cells: What it is
OpenAI's terminal coding agent; the same product also has an IDE extension, a desktop app, a web version and cloud tasks
Desktop and web workbench that runs Agent CLIs, Codex among them; not a model or an agent itself
Interface and platforms
Terminal UI plus `codex exec` for scripts; installers for macOS, Linux and Windows
Desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux; Docker Compose container; Microsoft Store edition
Pricing and licensing
CLI repository is Apache-2.0; usage comes with ChatGPT plans (Free, Go $8, Plus $20, Pro from $100 per month, as of October 2026) or API billing
Desktop and Container editions are free; Store edition is free with an optional one-time TurboEngine purchase
Model and provider access
OpenAI models through a ChatGPT sign-in or an API key; you choose model and reasoning effort
Hosts no models; uses whatever your Codex install is signed in to; optional OmniRoute model catalog
Parallel work
Subagents inside a session; `codex cloud` moves work to OpenAI's cloud
Several sessions side by side, each an Agent with a visible status
Spec and planning workflow
AGENTS.md via /init, permission levels via /permissions; no proposal archive of its own
OpenSpec proposals: propose, validate, apply, archive; free editions allow 3 concurrent proposals
Git and commit handling
/review checks uncommitted changes, a commit or a branch; docs suggest Git checkpoints around tasks
AI-composed commits, repository locked while committing, per-repo targeting with Monospecs
Setup effort
One installer, npm or Homebrew command, then sign in with ChatGPT or an API key
Needs Codex installed and signed in first, then HagiCode Desktop on top
Best for
Terminal users on a ChatGPT plan, scripts and CI
Parallel tasks, proposal-driven work and multi-repo projects

items.title: Open source, several ways to install
content: The Codex repository is published under the Apache-2.0 licence. You can install it with `npm install -g @openai/codex`, `brew install --cask codex`, or the standalone installer: `curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh` on macOS and Linux, and a PowerShell installer on Windows. Run `codex` in a project and choose Sign in with ChatGPT, or use an API key.

items.title: Your ChatGPT plan is the account
content: Codex is included in ChatGPT's plans, from Free and Go up to Plus, Pro, Business, Edu and Enterprise, and it shares usage limits with ChatGPT's other work features. An API key is the alternative for automation, billed at standard API rates and kept separate from subscription usage. That makes cost easy to reason about if you already pay for ChatGPT.

items.title: Control over what it may do
content: `/permissions` sets when Codex may edit files or run commands without asking, and shows the active sandbox and writable roots. You pick the model and reasoning effort per session. `/review` reviews uncommitted changes, a commit or a base branch without touching your working tree.

items.title: Built for scripts and delegation
content: `codex exec` runs non-interactive commands for CI and repeatable jobs, `codex mcp` adds MCP servers, `--search` turns on live web search, `--image` attaches a screenshot, and `codex resume` reopens saved chats. Codex can also hand focused work to subagents, and `codex cloud` moves a task to Codex in the cloud.

sections.title: When to choose Codex, and when to choose HagiCode

items: you already pay for a ChatGPT plan and want Codex included in it;
you want scripts and CI jobs through `codex exec` or an API key;
you prefer to control sandbox and approvals with `/permissions` and nothing else;
you like one terminal and a short install path with no extra application;
you want to hand work to Codex in the cloud with `codex cloud`.
you run several Codex tasks at once and want to see all of them in one place;
you want a reviewed proposal before the agent edits code, archived afterwards;
one Codex task spans several repositories and you would like them declared as one workspace;
you want Codex output turned into tidy commits, with a browser editor to fix what it got wrong;
you use Codex alongside other Agent CLIs and want one workspace.

blocks.title: Where HagiCode is not the right tool
content: CI and scripted one-shot runs should call `codex exec` directly; a desktop workbench adds nothing there.
If you want only a terminal and no GUI, or one quick question in an editor you already have open, HagiCode is more than you need.

HagiCode needs Codex installed and signed in first, so setup is longer than using Codex alone. Teams that do not want a proposal discipline will find it overhead, free editions cap concurrent proposals at 3, and the embedded Code Server editor is not a full IDE replacement.
Features that live in OpenAI's own surfaces, such as `codex cloud` and the IDE extension, stay there; HagiCode drives the local CLI.
HagiCode sits on top of the CLI. It runs your installed Codex through its SDK-backed integration, so your ChatGPT sign-in or API key, plan limits and billing stay with OpenAI.
Nothing is locked in. Your repositories, AGENTS.md and Codex configuration stay where they are, and you can run `codex` on the same project at any time.

items: Install Codex with npm, Homebrew or the standalone installer, and confirm it with `codex --version`.
Run `codex` once and sign in with ChatGPT or an API key, so it is authenticated before HagiCode uses it.
Install HagiCode Desktop for Windows, macOS or Linux, or use the Docker Compose or Microsoft Store edition.
In HagiCode's Agent CLI settings, pick Codex as the executor; HagiCode looks for the `codex` command on your PATH.
Open a repository and start a session or an OpenSpec proposal; Codex's tool calls appear in HagiCode's unified view.
To go back, close HagiCode and run `codex` in the same folder; nothing needs to be undone.

blocks.title: What works with Codex inside HagiCode
content: Parallel sessions, Agents management, OpenSpec proposals, AI commits, Code Server, Monospecs, Vault and the unified tool-call view work with Codex sessions.
Interactive questions are available only for Claude, Pi, OMP and Reasonix, and the agent work panel only for Claude Code, so neither appears for Codex.

sections.title: What HagiCode adds on top of any agent

items.title: Parallel sessions and Agents management
content: Each Codex session becomes an Agent with its own context and a visible status, so three Codex tasks in three folders are one list instead of three terminals.

items.title: OpenSpec proposals
content: A task can start as an OpenSpec proposal that you write, validate, apply and archive. Codex implements within it, and the proposal records why, which `codex resume` history alone does not.

items.title: AI commit and Code Server
content: HagiCode drafts the commit message from what Codex changed and locks the repository while committing. The embedded Code Server editor opens those files beside the conversation.

items.title: Monospecs and Vault
content: Monospecs lists the repositories of a multi-repo workspace so a Codex task knows about all of them. Vault keeps reference code and notes available to later sessions, which a new `codex` run would start without.

items.title: Model routing, tool-call view and usage
content: Codex's tool calls are shown in the same typed shape as every other CLI, live and in history. OmniRoute can supply a model catalog per Agent CLI, and an optional TokenMonitor readout in the status bar shows today's tokens and cost.

items: Codex is the agent in your terminal; HagiCode is the workbench that runs it.
Stay with Codex alone for solo, single-task or scripted work on your ChatGPT plan; add HagiCode for parallel tasks, proposals and multi-repo changes.
Codex must be installed and signed in first, and you can go back to running `codex` directly at any time.

faq.question: How do I install Codex?
faq.answer: Run `npm install -g @openai/codex` or `brew install --cask codex`. The standalone installer for macOS and Linux is `curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh`, and Windows has a PowerShell installer in the repository README at github.com/openai/codex. Then run `codex` and sign in.

faq.question: Is Codex free?
faq.answer: The CLI itself is open source under Apache-2.0, but use needs a ChatGPT plan or an API key. As of October 2026 OpenAI lists Codex in ChatGPT Free, Go ($8), Plus ($20) and higher plans; API-key use is billed at API rates.

faq.question: Can I use Codex with HagiCode?
faq.answer: Yes. Install and sign in to Codex, then choose it as the Agent CLI in HagiCode. Your ChatGPT sign-in or API key and its billing stay with OpenAI.

faq.question: Does HagiCode replace Codex?
faq.answer: No. HagiCode runs Codex as its executor and adds sessions, proposals, commits and multi-repo tools around it. You can still run `codex` on the same repositories.

faq.question: Does Codex work on Windows?
faq.answer: OpenAI provides a PowerShell installer for Windows in the Codex README. Check the Codex documentation for current Windows notes before relying on it.

faq.question: Codex vs HagiCode: which should I pick?
faq.answer: Pick Codex alone for terminal, solo or CI work on your ChatGPT plan. Add HagiCode when you want parallel sessions, OpenSpec proposals or multi-repo workspaces on top of Codex.
